title: The River That Ran Backward
summary: Everyone in Stillmouth throws into the river whatever they want to be rid of, and the river carries it away. But when Tomé's grandmother goes upriver by mistake, he discovers there's a place where the river gives everything back — and that reaching it means going against the current of his own memory.

chapters.title: What the Current Carries
chapters.body:
In Stillmouth, when someone wanted to be rid of a thing, they threw it into the river.

Not trash — for trash there was the deep well behind the church. The river was for something else. It was for what hurt. A letter that shouldn't have been written, a dead brother's toy, the portrait of a love that had turned to bitterness. A person would go to the stone bridge at nightfall, hold the thing in their hands until they found the courage, and let go. And the river of Stillmouth — which was a strange river, dark and smooth as glass — carried it away. Not downstream, like any river. The river of Stillmouth ran from the sea to the mountain, opposite to every other river in the world, and what fell into it rose, and rose, until it vanished into the mist of the highlands from which no one had ever returned.

People said this was a blessing. Throw your pain into the river and it carries it far away, up high, to where you'll never have to look at it again. And it worked — more or less. People felt lighter afterward. Only they also felt a hole, and the hole didn't close, it just got easier to ignore.

Tomé was thirteen years old and lived with his grandmother, Fé, in a little house near the bank. His parents had gone away — not by the river, but the ordinary way, one to the other side of the country in search of work, and then the silence, and then the letters growing scarce. Fé raised him. She was a small, stubborn old woman, with the rough hands of a washerwoman and a memory that, lately, had begun to slip through her fingers like water.

That was the trouble. For months now Fé had been forgetting things. Where she'd put her glasses. What day it was. Sometimes she called Tomé by her son's name, and sometimes she looked at him with the frightened eyes of someone who has woken in a strange place. The neighbors shook their heads and said it was her age, that her mind was going upriver the way everything in Stillmouth went.

And then, on a foggy morning, Fé was gone.

Tomé woke and her bed was cold. The door, open. And on the bank, by the stone bridge, her slippers, side by side, very neatly placed, the way you leave your shoes before stepping into a place.

A neighbor, Mrs. Bela, found him standing there, staring at the smooth, dark water.

"Oh, my boy," she said, and her voice was full of the pity we reserve for what cannot be mended. "She'd grown so confused, poor thing. She must have… must have gotten muddled. Thought she was a thing to throw away." Mrs. Bela pulled her shawl tight around her shoulders. "She went into the river, child. And the river… you know. The river takes."

"And doesn't give back?" Tomé asked.

Mrs. Bela was slow to answer. And when she answered, it was in a whisper, glancing around like someone telling a forbidden thing:

"They say there's a place," she said. "Up in the highlands, at the spring that runs backward. They say that's where the river keeps everything it has carried. Everything Stillmouth has thrown away in a hundred years. And they say" — she swallowed hard — "that whoever reaches it can take one thing back. Just one. But no one has ever reached it, Tomé. Because to climb the river backward, you don't walk against the water. You walk against something else. And most people can't bear it."

"Against what?" Tomé asked.

But Mrs. Bela only shook her head, and wouldn't say, and went off wiping her eyes.

Tomé looked at his grandmother's empty slippers. He looked at the dark river rising in silence toward the shrouded highlands. And he went home to make a bundle of food, because he had already decided, there on the bank, that he was going to bring his grandmother back — even though no one had ever returned, even without knowing what he would have to fight.

chapters.title: Against the Current
chapters.body:
Tomé followed the river upward.

The first day was easy. The bank was firm, the river ran gentle and dark beside him, always rising, and he walked with the bundle on his back and his determination whole. He passed the last house of Stillmouth, passed the abandoned mill, passed to where the fields gave way to the thick brush of the highlands.

It was on the second day, when the river began to truly climb, up into the mountains, that Tomé understood what Mrs. Bela had meant.

Walking against that river did not tire the legs. It tired the memory.

The higher he climbed, the more the river ran backward — and not only the water. Time, there, also ran in reverse. Tomé began to remember things backward. First the recent ones: he remembered Fé disappearing, then Fé confused, then Fé still clear-minded, teaching him to fish. The memories came in reversed order, unwinding the thread of his life backward.

And it hurt. Because to remember backward is to relive things knowing how they end. Tomé remembered a happy day at the fair with his grandmother — and now, climbing the river, he felt the happiness of that day together with the weight of knowing everything that came after. The good memories, in reverse, turned bittersweet. The bad ones turned worse.

Higher up, the river began to show things. On the smooth, dark water passed, rising, all the things Stillmouth had thrown away. Tomé saw notes, portraits, toys, wedding rings, letters — all floating upward, toward the spring. And sometimes the water showed, like a mirror, the scenes in which those things had been thrown: people crying on the bridge, letting go of what they loved, turning their backs lighter and emptier.

There was a terrible temptation in that. Because the river, Tomé began to realize, offered him a silent bargain with every step. "Does it hurt to remember your grandmother?" the water seemed to whisper. "Does it hurt to carry all of this uphill? You don't have to. Throw it in the river. Throw the memory of her in and the pain goes away. You'll feel light. Everyone does it."

And that was it — Tomé understood suddenly — that kept people from reaching the spring. It was not the climb. It was that, to climb the river backward, you had to relive all your pain in reverse, without letting go of a single piece of it on the way. And at any moment you could stop suffering: you only had to give the river the very person you had come to find. Most, at some point in the climb, tired and hurt, threw the memory into the water and went back down relieved and empty, no longer even remembering why they had begun to climb.

The river wanted Tomé to forget Fé. That was the toll. And the higher he went, the cheaper the river made it seem.

On the third night, exhausted, soaked, his head pounding with relived memories, Tomé sat on the bank and nearly gave in. A memory had just come — the oldest and the most painful, from the very bottom: himself very small, his parents still home, driving away down the road, and Fé holding his hand at the door, saying "I'm staying, my love, I'm not going anywhere." To relive that in reverse — to feel his parents' abandonment arriving instead of departing — was almost too much.

"Throw it in the river," the water whispered, gentle, dark, so easy. "Throw the old woman in. You barely remember her voice anymore. Throw it in and go down. Feel light."

And Tomé, with tears running down, nearly reached out toward the water.

But then he remembered — not in reverse, but the right way, because some memories are too strong for the river to invert — that very promise. "I'm staying. I'm not going anywhere." Fé had stayed. When everyone went away, she stayed. And now it was his turn.

"No," Tomé said to the river, and drew his hand back from the water. "You're not taking her too. She stayed with me. I'm going to stay with her."

And he got up, and went on climbing, carrying every memory that hurt as if it were stones in his pockets, without letting go of a single one — because he had understood, at last, that this was exactly what the river couldn't bear: someone who would rather carry the pain than forget the one they loved.

chapters.title: The Spring That Gives Back
chapters.body:
On the fourth day, Tomé reached the spring.

It was not what he had imagined. There was no cave, no treasure, no monster. There was only a small, perfectly round lake, high in the mountains, ringed by pale stones and by a mist that glowed faintly, as if it held light. And the lake was the spring in reverse: instead of water welling up from it and flowing down, the water climbed the whole river and plunged in there, vanishing into the earth in a silent whirlpool. Everything Stillmouth had thrown away in a hundred years floated on that lake — a gentle multitude of portraits and letters and toys and memories, turning slowly on the surface, waiting.

And on a stone at the lake's edge, her bare feet in the water and a calm about her that Tomé had not seen in months, sat Fé.

"Gran!" Tomé ran and hugged her, and she was solid, and warm, and real.

"My Tomé," she said, and her voice was clear, and her eyes were lucid, more lucid than they had been in a long time. "You climbed the river. My goodness, boy. You climbed the whole river."

"I came for you," he said. "Let's go home."

But Fé held his face in her rough hands and looked at him with a sweet sadness, and Tomé felt, before she spoke, that something was not going to be simple.

"Listen, my love," she said. "I didn't fall into the river by mistake." She saw the confusion on his face and went on, slowly. "For months now my mind has been going, Tomé. You saw it. I forget things. I forget you, sometimes, and it breaks my heart every time I come back and realize it. And I got afraid. Afraid that one day I'd forget for good, and become a burden, and you'd have to care for an old woman who no longer even knows who you are." Her eyes filled. "So I came to the river. Not to throw myself away. I came here, to the spring, because I knew the legend. Up here, my memory comes back. You saw how I am. Lucid. Whole. The river gives back everything it has carried — and it was carrying my forgettings upriver, one by one. Here at the spring they've been given back to me. Here I am myself again."

Tomé began to understand, and the understanding was terrible.

"Then stay," he said. "Stay here, where you remember."

"No one can live at the spring, my love," said Fé, with infinite tenderness. "Here time runs backward. I would stay lucid, yes, but I would also grow younger each day, going back, and back, until I became a child, until I became nothing. This is not a place to live. It is a place to choose." She pointed at the lake full of floating things. "The legend is true. Whoever reaches here can take one thing back. Just one." She took his hands. "You can take me, Tomé. As I am now, lucid. But if you take me, you'll also take everything that came with me — the illness, the forgettings, the fear. Down below, with time running right again, I'll go back to forgetting. Maybe faster. And one day, not far off, I'll forget you for good, and you'll have to care for me until the end, without my even being able to say thank you."

She squeezed his hands.

"Or," she said, very softly, "you can leave me here. Let the spring take me into the earth, slowly, lucid, without fear and without pain. And take back home, in my place, something else from this lake. Anything. Your parents' letters, which I threw into the river years ago because they made me cry. Your mother's portrait. Something to make you lighter. And go on with your life without the weight of an old woman fading away."

Tomé looked at the lake. He looked at his parents' letters floating there, which he hadn't even known existed. He looked at his grandmother, lucid and whole and ready to depart in peace. And he understood that this was the choice the river made with everyone, all the time, down below at the stone bridge: let go of what hurts and be light, or carry what you love and be whole.

He had already answered that question on the third night, on the bank, when he drew his hand back from the water. And he answered it again now.

"I didn't climb this whole river to come back with a portrait, Gran," he said, and he was crying, but smiling. "I climbed it to find you. I want you. However it comes. Lucid or forgetting, light or heavy. You stayed with me when everyone went away. Now I stay with you. To the end. Even if the end is you forgetting my name. I'll know yours. That's enough for the both of us."

Fé cried, and hugged him, and for a long moment the two of them stayed there, at the edge of the glowing spring, high on the only river in the world that ran backward.

Then she stood up. She took her grandson's hand. And the two of them began to descend.

The descent was quick — the river, which makes the climb so hard, does nothing against those who go down; perhaps it even helps, relieved to see someone leaving with what they came for. Tomé's memories wound back into the right order. The pain he had carried uphill stayed in his pockets, but lighter now, the way pain becomes lighter when you stop running from it.

Fé went back to forgetting, in time. It was as she had warned. Some days she called Tomé by her son's name; on others, she looked at him without knowing who he was. But every day, without fail, Tomé sat with her on the porch, facing the dark river that climbed toward the highlands, and told her who she was, and who he was, and the story of the two of them. "You're Fé," he'd say. "And you stayed with me when everyone went away. And I climbed a whole river for you. And I'm staying."

And even on the days when she didn't understand the words, she smiled — because some things we recognize without needing memory, and the love of someone who stays is one of them.

They say in Stillmouth that Tomé was the only person who climbed the river backward and came home. And when people ask him what's up there at the spring, what treasure, what secret, he always answers the same thing:

"There's a choice. And most people choose wrong because wrong is lighter." And then he looks toward the porch, where an old woman dozes in the sun without remembering her own name, and smiles. "But light isn't the same thing as right."
